Making AI model access understandable

As AI models are shared across enterprise teams, administrators have to piece together permissions, usage limits, and model configuration to understand who can use what. I redesigned governance in Red Hat OpenShift AI around those relationships, giving administrators a connected way to audit access, trace problems, and spot gaps in the setup.

Primary UX Designer
Timeline
2 months
Product
Red Hat OpenShift AI

The challenge

Administrators had to piece together models, groups, permissions, and usage limits across separate pages. That made incomplete setup hard to spot and urgent access problems harder to investigate.

My contribution

I led the workflow workshop, reframed the problem, explored and tested interactive directions, revised the navigation, and partnered with product, engineering, UX, and customer-facing specialists.

What shipped

A new Overview page, updated MaaS Governance navigation, and refreshed Subscription and Authorization Policy settings pages.

Confidentiality note

Some details are omitted or generalized. Examples use illustrative models and groups. This account describes my contribution; the analysis and opinions are my own.

01 Context

Two settings determine access to a shared model

Red Hat OpenShift AI (RHOAI) helps organizations develop, deploy, and manage AI models. Its Models-as-a-Service (MaaS) capability lets teams use shared language models through governed access. Administrators manage access for user groups, which can represent teams within an organization.

For a group to use an available model, two settings must line up. An authorization policy permits the group to use the model’s endpoint, the address an application sends requests to. A subscription gives that group a usage allowance for the model. Token rate limits control how much text it can process over time.

Neither setting alone tells the full story. An administrator needs to see the model, group, authorization policy, and subscription together to understand whether access has been configured.

02 Discovery

The brief described separate pages. The workflow revealed a larger problem.

Start with the whole journey

The brief pointed to similar-looking Subscription and Authorization Policy tables on separate pages. Administrators opened details, remembered names, switched pages, and compared them manually. My initial hypothesis was that administrators struggled because Subscription and Authorization Policy information was separated across Settings. That described the interface, but it did not yet explain which relationships mattered in a real investigation or what someone needed to do next.

I led a workshop with product managers, engineers, and a UX colleague. Using existing research personas, I mapped the journey from making a model available to configuring access, using it, and investigating problems. I drafted job stories with Cursor, then edited them for accuracy. In the workshop we challenged assumptions, identified gaps, and prioritized opportunities; people who could not attend could add to the Miro board afterward.

Test the assumptions with people close to customers

The workshop exposed more than a page-switching problem. A newly published model could be missing one or both access settings, yet administrators had no single place to see that gap. The model’s availability also lived outside the Settings area. In the resource tables, counts hid group and model names in small, scrollable popovers. Those choices made it difficult to scan coverage, especially as the number of models and groups grew.

Creation forms raised a related problem: administrators could not see the corresponding policy or subscription while filling one out. They could duplicate coverage, create only part of a group–model relationship, or finish one form thinking access was ready. I explored those form opportunities, but the investigation view became the priority.

To make those possibilities concrete, I rapidly prototyped several screens and reviewed them with a Principal UX Designer. We compared a topology-style relationship map and table-based approaches, weighed how quickly each could lead to an answer, and narrowed the options before speaking with a Field and Customer Adoption specialist. The prototype was a way to test our understanding, not a final answer.

In that conversation, a real escalation sharpened the need: users might report that their group had run out of tokens, and an administrator needed to find its allowance and the relevant settings quickly. The specialist helped us focus on the questions the interface had to answer: “Who can use this model?” and “What can this team use?”

03 The problem

Administrators needed a way to trace access, not just compare tables

When an administrator needs to configure or troubleshoot access to a shared AI model, they need to see which groups can use it, what limits apply, and which setting is missing or needs attention. That relationship was spread across separate views, forcing them to reconstruct it from memory before they could act.

The most urgent cases started with a model or a group. A useful view had to show the connections from either starting point, distinguish complete from incomplete setup, and lead to the underlying subscription or policy. It also had to work when many models and groups were involved.

04 Design decisions

Make the relationships visible, then let people follow the detail

Organize the page around the administrator’s question

I proposed one MaaS Governance area with an Overview and supporting Subscriptions and Authorization Policies tabs. The Overview would group information by model or by group, matching the two questions from discovery. The existing resource views would remain available for someone who already knew which subscription or policy they wanted to inspect.

Weigh the alternatives

I explored side-by-side governance cards, compound table expansion, and a topology-style map. The map made connections explicit but added navigation complexity. The table-based Overview offered a clearer path to investigation: an administrator could start with a Model or Group, expand a row, and compare subscriptions and authorization policies in one place. The two perspectives answered complementary questions without changing the underlying relationship model.

Check the data and feasibility

Engineering had to validate the data shape. The underlying services list subscriptions and policies, each naming models; they do not return a model with all its access settings attached. Frontend and backend engineers confirmed a joined Overview was feasible without a visibly slow page. That let us choose the clearer interaction rather than letting the API structure dictate the interface.

Show the exact group relationship

An Overview count could say a model had both kinds of setting while concealing that they covered different groups. I made group names visible in the expanded row and added a way to select one. Selecting a group highlights its matching subscription and authorization policy cards, so an administrator can follow that group to its allowance and permission without losing the surrounding context. This helps locate configuration; it does not show live token consumption.

I iterated on the card structure, expansion behavior, labels, color, and spacing to keep the view scannable. The interaction emerged from the escalation scenario: finding the affected group quickly was more important than simply displaying every relationship at once.

Give each supporting table a clear job

The Overview explains relationships. The Subscriptions and Authorization Policies tabs let administrators inspect a known setting. For those tables, I compared side-by-side cards with PatternFly compound expansion, an existing product pattern that reveals details within the table row. Customer-facing reviewers preferred expansion here: it kept the surrounding rows visible while they inspected group and model names. The Overview used expansion for a different purpose: to compare connected resources and trace relationships.

I also explored creation-form improvements, including showing related settings while someone edits and helping prevent partial coverage. We prioritized the Overview and supporting resource tables; broader form changes remained a separate opportunity. Teams using GitOps, where configuration is managed through version-controlled files, raised another practical need: the underlying YAML configuration file had to remain easy to reach from the relevant resource.

05 Delivery

Prioritize the core investigation and refine it through feedback

In a weekly UX, product, and engineering review, we checked feasibility, agreed on the revised navigation, and broke the work into deliverable pieces. The Overview was the first priority, with Model and Group perspectives tied to the questions from discovery. I shared working prototypes so reviewers could expand rows, filter results, and try the group-highlighting behavior rather than judging static screens alone.

Cursor let me make several interaction ideas tangible quickly. The framing and decisions came from the workshop, specialist feedback, design critique, and engineering review.

I then refined the Model and Group rows, resource cards, configuration states, and supporting tables with engineering and Content Design. Customer-facing specialists responded strongly to the Overview and helped us select the compound expansion pattern for the resource tables. Early feedback made it possible to improve the design while it could still change.

I separated the relationship-focused Overview from the supporting resource tables in handoff. Form improvements remained a distinct opportunity, while the core investigation flow stayed focused on the questions administrators needed to answer.

06 Outcome

A clearer path from an access question to the setting behind it

The redesigned MaaS Governance experience brought access relationships into an Overview, alongside improved Subscription and Authorization Policy tables. The design supports Model and Group perspectives so an administrator can begin with the question they have, inspect related settings, trace matching labels and cards, and identify incomplete configuration without comparing separate resource pages.

Customer-facing specialists welcomed the direction, especially the ability to inspect access relationships without reconstructing them across pages.

I estimated the potential audience at more than 1,000 RHOAI administrators globally. Red Hat does not publicly disclose a global administrator count, so this is an approximate audience estimate, not a usage or outcome metric. I do not yet have reliable task-success data, so I cannot claim a measured reduction in troubleshooting time or configuration errors.

The next evaluation should observe administrators completing real tasks: identify a group’s access, find an incomplete connection, and locate its usage limit. Task success, time, and confidence would show whether the new view delivers the improvement it was designed for.
